claims.text: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is primarily governed by thermally activated local phase heterogeneities.
Local phase heterogeneities produce microscale thermal-expansion mismatch.
Microscale thermal-expansion mismatch generates internal residual stresses.
The mismatch-induced internal stresses affect creep, hardness evolution, and elastic moduli.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr has a nominally homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
Changing thermal ramp rate and hold time at 600–800 °C can modulate local phase separation in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed structural mediator consists of nanoscale compositional or phase domains having thermal-expansion coefficients different from that of the matrix.
High-temperature diffusion promotes slight local phase decomposition or chemical ordering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal cycling or mechanical loading of regions with different thermal-expansion behavior produces heterogeneous residual stresses.
Relative to a uniform baseline, enhanced local phase heterogeneity will increase the high-temperature creep rate.
Enhanced local phase heterogeneity will produce localized hardening after aging at 600–800 °C.
Enhanced local phase heterogeneity will cause deviations in elastic-modulus trends over 293–1100 K.
Introducing spatially inhomogeneous thermal-expansion coefficients in a simulation will redistribute internal stresses in a way that matches experimental trends.
An alloy condition with minimized compositional fluctuations will have nearly uniform thermal-expansion properties.
Thermal-heterogeneity effects will be most pronounced near or above 600 °C and during tensile creep at approximately 1250 °C.
At temperatures well below 600 °C, the effects will diminish because thermal activation is insufficient to drive significant phase separation.
